opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a fun question, because poker has been a kind of personal benchmark for me for a long time. When I was working on Libratus and later Pluribus, the striking thing was how much of the performance came from search, from letting the system think at the moment it had to make a decision, rather than just from a bigger pre-trained policy. Adding real-time search was worth far more than scaling up the model by orders of magnitude. That lesson shaped a lot of how I think about reasoning in language models.

So when I look at today's models, one test I find useful is whether they can work through the kind of problem you face when building a solver. Can they reason about counterfactual regret minimization, figure out why an implementation isn't converging, spot that you're computing reach probabilities wrong, or think through abstraction choices for a big game? A few years ago, models could recite the textbook description of CFR but would fall apart as soon as you asked them to debug real code or handle the subtle game-theoretic issues. They'd produce something that looked right and wasn't.

Now, with models that think for a while before answering, it's noticeably different. They can hold a longer chain of reasoning together, catch their own mistakes, and say, "wait, that's not right, the opponent's strategy has to be fixed here," and backtrack. That self-correction is the qualitative shift. It's the same thing we saw in poker: giving the system time to think at inference changes what it can do.

They're not perfect. They still sometimes go confidently down the wrong path, and in imperfect-information settings especially, intuitions from perfect-information games can mislead them. But the trajectory is really clear, and honestly faster than I expected. Things I'd have said would take a strong PhD student a week, the models can now make serious progress on in a single session. For me, that's the most convincing evidence that reasoning is improving, not just knowledge retrieval.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the poker experience really shaped how I look at this. When I was working on poker, the thing that became clear to me was that the models we were building, the neural nets, were basically operating on intuition. You'd train them on a bunch of data and they'd give you an instant answer. And that worked okay, but the breakthrough in poker was really when we added search, when we gave the system the ability to think for a while before acting. We saw that if you let the bot think for, like, 20 or 30 seconds instead of acting instantly, it was the equivalent of scaling up the model by something like a thousand times. That was a huge, huge result, and honestly it kind of shocked me at the time.

So when I look at the progress in reasoning in language models, I'm judging it through that lens. For a long time, these models were essentially just doing the intuition part. You ask a question, you get the first thing that comes out, and that's the equivalent of a poker player going on gut feel every single hand. And they were pretty good at it! But they were brittle in exactly the ways you'd expect: they'd make errors on things that a bit of deliberation would catch.

What's changed is that we now have models that can actually spend compute at inference time, that can think longer about harder problems. And the thing I find most striking is that it generalizes. In poker, the search was very domain-specific. It worked for poker, and it worked for Go, but you couldn't take the poker search algorithm and point it at a math problem. Now you have one approach that works across math, coding, science, and it keeps improving the longer you let it think. That's the signal I watch for. Not whether the model gets a particular question right, but whether performance keeps climbing as you give it more time to reason. If that curve is still going up, we're not close to done.

astra-6.text:
Poker gives you a useful perspective because it separates knowing what a good decision looks like from actually working through a hard decision. You can train a model to recognize patterns and produce a pretty good answer immediately, but there’s also the question of how much better it can do if you give it time to think.

In poker, that second part was incredibly important. You wouldn’t expect a strong human player to spend the same amount of time on every decision. Some situations are straightforward; others deserve a lot of thought. I think we should expect something similar from AI.

So when I judge progress in reasoning, I’m interested in more than whether the next model gets a higher score. Does giving it more time actually improve its decisions? Can it identify a mistake, reconsider an assumption, and arrive at a better answer? And does that work on problems it hasn’t effectively seen before?

The encouraging thing about poker was that you didn’t need to anticipate every situation during training. Computation at decision time could make up a lot of the difference. The harder question for language models is how to get that benefit when the rules are less explicit and checking an answer isn’t as straightforward.

sol-6.1.text:
Poker taught me to distinguish between a system that recognizes a familiar pattern and one that can work through a situation it hasn’t seen before. You can get quite far by learning what a good player would do. But some of the biggest improvements came from giving the system time to reason about the particular decision in front of it.

That’s a useful lens for language models. We often focus on how much compute goes into training, but there’s also the question of how effectively a model can use compute when answering a question. Can it consider different approaches, catch a mistake, and revise its answer? If you give it more time, does it reliably get better?

The important caveat is that poker gives you a very precise framework for doing that. You know the rules, the possible actions, and what winning means. With a general-purpose model, even figuring out whether an answer is correct can be difficult. So I’m encouraged by progress on problems where we can check the result, but I’d be careful about assuming that success there automatically translates into reliable reasoning everywhere.
